analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada and other countries at lower prices.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill with 29 cosponsors to let Americans import cheaper prescription drugs never received a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal drug law to allow pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals to import prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries, where the same FDA-approved medicines routinely sell for far less. It set up a registration and inspection system for importers and exporters, required track-and-trace records, and made it illegal for drug manufacturers to cut off supply to, or charge higher prices to, anyone importing drugs into the United States. The bill was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay for prescription drugs, especially the uninsured and underinsured, plus seniors on fixed incomes. The bill's own findings state that Americans pay up to five times more for the same medicines than consumers abroad, and that prescription drugs cost 35 to 55 percent less in other developed countries. It also lets U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers act as registered importers, giving them a legal path to buy lower-priced drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Waits on the current ban: the bill repeals the existing restriction on importing drugs that were originally exported from the United States, allowing reimportation of FDA-approved medicines from registered sources abroad.

Limits personal importation to qualifying drugs with a U.S.-approved equivalent, capped at a 90-day supply with a valid prescription, and excludes controlled substances, biologics, injected drugs, and other higher-risk categories.

Requires every registered importer and exporter to submit to FDA registration, facility inspections, chain-of-custody verification, tamper-resistant and anti-counterfeiting markings, and recall coordination, with FDA inspectors visiting exporter premises at least 12 times a year.

Makes it unlawful for manufacturers to discriminate against importers by charging them higher prices, denying or delaying supply, or causing differences between the U.S. version of a drug and the version sold abroad, with the Federal Trade Commission empowered to seek triple damages.

States that reselling in the U.S. a drug properly sold abroad is not patent infringement, and requires the Secretary to publish a public list of registered exporters so consumers know which sellers are legitimate.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose revenue as Americans buy the same medicines at lower foreign prices, and who would bear the cost of the notice, inspection, and supply-continuity requirements designed to stop them from blocking importation. The program is funded by registration and inspection fees paid by importers and exporters.

drawbacks.text: Importing drugs from foreign supply chains carries safety risks: drugs can be counterfeit, damaged, or mishandled, and verifying every shipment is hard. The bill responds with registration, inspections, chain-of-custody verification, and anti-counterfeiting markings, but no screening regime is airtight and FDA oversight would depend on adequate funding and staffing.

Drug makers would have strong incentives to fight back by restricting supply to Canada and other permitted countries, as they did in earlier importation disputes. The bill makes that unlawful and gives the FTC enforcement power, but the effectiveness of those anti-discrimination rules would be untested in practice.

Consumers buying directly from an online exporter receive drugs not repackaged to U.S. pharmacy standards unless they consent to compliant packaging, and personal imports come with advisories where the foreign version differs in inactive ingredients or is not bioequivalent to the U.S. version.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Americans paying some of the highest drug prices in the world, the potential savings are large, and the bill's registration, inspection, and track-and-trace system is a serious attempt to manage the real safety risks rather than ignore them. The honest cost side is that the safety regime is unproven at scale, manufacturers would likely test the anti-supply-cutoff rules in court, and FDA would need steady funding and staffing the bill provides only through fees. On balance it is a carefully structured attempt at a widely desired change, and its death without any hearing or vote means those design questions were never answered in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced in March 2009, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 4, 2009 by Senator Byron Dorgan (D-ND) with an unusual bipartisan group of initial cosponsors including Republicans Olympia Snowe, Chuck Grassley, John McCain, Susan Collins, and John Thune, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Twenty-nine senators cosponsored the bill: 22 of 58 Senate Democrats, 6 of 40 Senate Republicans, and the chamber's 1 Independent.

The action history shows no activity after the committee referral and the sponsor's introductory remarks in early March 2009; there was no hearing, no committee vote, and no Senate floor action recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

The bill's stated purpose was to address Americans paying up to five times more to fill prescriptions than consumers in other countries, with drugs costing 35 to 55 percent less in other developed countries according to the Congressional Budget Office.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the existing ban on cheaper drug importation and the pricing structure that goes with it, since the bill never advanced far enough to threaten their U.S. revenue.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction: 22 of 58 Senate Democrats, 6 of 40 Senate Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent cosponsored it, so the failure to advance cannot be explained by party opposition alone.

industries.note: The bill would open the U.S. market to the same drugs sold at 35 to 55 percent lower prices abroad, cutting into manufacturer revenue, and its anti-discrimination provisions are aimed squarely at preventing manufacturers from cutting off foreign supply to stop importation. Higher U.S. prices are what fund the industry's other markets, so its interest runs against American consumers here.

industries.industry: Internet and mail-order pharmacies, especially Canadian ones
industries.note: Registered exporters, many of them existing Canadian online pharmacies, would gain a legal, FDA-supervised channel to sell into the U.S. market. Consumers get cheaper drugs; the pharmacies get a legitimate business.

The bill lets U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers register as importers and buy qualifying drugs abroad, passing some of the price gap to their customers. They would also pay registration and inspection fees capped at 2.5 percent of import value.
The bill funds new FDA and Customs inspection and tracking work through fees on importers and exporters, expanding the agencies' role in verifying drug shipments.
